physical.physical_description: Skirt cloth (Kain panjang) of batik on machine made tabby weave cotton cloth. With a design in the main field which consists of alternate rows of blue and cream diamonds, each with an individualised bird or crayfish design. The body of the cloth is flanked by two end panels with contrasting grounds of blue, red and white, including a rectangular section with bird and crayfish designs, rows of tumpal or triangle designs and, at the end, scattered floral motifs.
physical.summary: Batik is the name given in Indonesia to the process of applying resist-dyed patterns to cloth. Batik patterned cloths are worn by both men and women in Java, the kain panjang being the skirt or waist cloth worn by men. The main centres of production were the areas around the Sultanates of Surakarta and Jogyakarta or Yogyakarta in central Java, and the coastal areas of Cirebon, Indramayu, Pekalongan and Lasem in the north and the area around Garut in western Java. Colour combinations of blue and white, red and white, and red and blue, as found in this example, which was probably made in Cirebon, were common in batik cloths from the northern coastal area which had always been subject to considerable influence from external trade, both from the east (China) and the west (India).

physical.physical_description: Skirt cloth (kain panjang) of cotton batik in the pagi-sore (morning/evening) style. It has different designs at each end so that it can be worn on different occasions. One end has a rice grain background on a cream ground with floral and leaf designs in bright blue, and red, with yellow leaves. The other end has a blue background with semen and rambling foliage in mustard colour with large crysanthemum type flowers in blue and red and leaves with yellow veins on a red background. The overall design consists of four floral bouquets, two at each end, and a partial bouquet straddling the centre.
physical.summary: This cotton batik kain panjang of the so-called morning/evening type has different designs at each end so that it can be worn on different occasions--for morning or evening functions, for example. The design itself is referred to as the Hokokai style, and is of a type commonly made in the period of the Japanese occupation of Java. One end has a rice grain background on a cream ground with floral and leaf designs in bright blue, and red, with yellow leaves. The other end has a blue background, a background of rambling foliage in mustard colour and, superimposed, large crysanthemum type flowers in blue and red and leaves with yellow veins on red background. The overall design consists of four floral bouquets, two at each end, and a partial bouquet straddling the centre.

physical.physical_description: Skirt cloth (Kain panjang) with a batik pattern on machine made tabby weave cotton cloth. The basic structure of the design consists of a ground with a loose  patchwork of traditional central Javanese designs. Superimposed on that background is a menagerie of wild animals and birds (elephants, leopards or tigers, deer, swan-like birds), a type of design known as kebun binatang or animal garden. The whole design direction is reversed half way through the cloth, making it technically a cloth of the type known as pagi-sore or morning-evening cloth.
physical.summary: Batik is the Indonesian name for the process of applying resist-dyed patterns to cloth. The principal places of manufacture are the areas around the Sultanates of Surakarta and Yogyakarta in central Java, some of the coastal towns of the north, such as Cirebon, Lasem, Pekalongan and Indramayu, and the area around Garut in western Java. The traditional batiks from the manufacturing centres in central Java are distinct from those in the other areas and typically show a restrained range of colours--rich browns, indigo blue, cream, white and black being the main elements of the palette. This batik, which is in the form of a kain panjang, or man's skirt cloth, has all the hallmarks of a central Javanese example, including a loose patchwork background of traditional central Javanese designs. Superimposed on that is a menagerie of wild animals and birds (elephants, leopards or tigers, deer, swanlike birds)--a type of design known as kebun binatang or animal garden. Further, the whole design direction is reversed half way through the cloth, making it technically a cloth of the type known as pagi-sore--a cloth that can be reversed for wearing either in the morning or the evening.
